title: Choose who, not just what.
description: You cannot decide every detail in advance when building something difficult. Jensen explains why choosing the people matters.

transcript: You gotta go through thick and thin.
There are a lot of unpredictable things in the future.
And it's because you're building a chip together. It's a foundry.
It's not exactly like buying something off the shelf.
You're building a chip together, and it's really hard to build chips.
So it's impossible to know all the details.
It's impossible to make all the decisions up front.
You really are choosing not...
what to buy, but who to work with.

reviewNote: The chip-building example explains the conclusion. A finished product can be specified in advance; a difficult collaboration keeps producing decisions that nobody could fully anticipate. Jensen is describing why a partner's judgment and values matter when the written plan runs out.

title: Why 74 days? Why not six?
description: Question the starting point before improving the process. A fresh analysis reveals what is possible and which tradeoffs explain the rest.

transcript: I don't like going into a problem, and somebody says,
It takes 74 days to do this today.
And we can do it for you in 72 days.
I'd rather strip it all back to zero
First of all, explain to me
why 74 days in the first place.
Let's think about what's possible today.
And if I were to build it completely from scratch,
How long would it take?
Oftentimes, you'd be surprised.
It might come to six days.
Now, the rest of the six days, the 74, could be
very well reasoned, and compromises,
cost reductions, and all kinds of different things.
But at least you know what they are.
Now that you know that six days is possible,
then the conversation from 74 to six,
surprisingly much more effective.

reviewNote: The six day result is a hypothetical example, not a measured productivity claim. The useful step is to separate physical possibilities from inherited assumptions, then identify which real costs and compromises explain the remaining time. The clip keeps that qualification.

title: The kindness behind the street food
description: After a night market visit, Jensen notices the generosity of people who work hard and take pride in their craft.

transcript: Everybody's working hard for a living, and they're working so hard,
and they still want to share a little something with you.
They don't have that much money.
Their profit margin on that thing must be a dime each.
They gave me all their profit, right?
Just to be kind.
It's the Taiwanese way,
and it's nice to watch these people, their craft.

reviewNote: His attention shifts from the food to the people doing the work. The remark about a dime of profit is his estimate, not a verified margin. The moment is revealing because he notices the generosity of a small gesture as well as the skill behind it.

title: The beauty of imperfection
description: A spontaneous aside at Computex about learning to appreciate imperfection and the beauty of things that are one of a kind.

transcript: Look at that. That's beautiful.
When I was young, I would think that that's not good.
But now, I love wabi-sabi.
Beautiful things... imperfect.
I love that.
Imperfection is beauty.
Look at that. One of a kind.

reviewNote: This is a spontaneous reflection on how his taste has changed, rather than a formal design rule. He is responding to a display and appreciating something singular. The short exchange leaves room for imperfection without claiming to identify a particular defect.

title: First, breakfast. Then, TSMC.
description: Lex tries to return to the TSMC story. Jensen has a delicious reason to pause. A small, unguarded moment over breakfast.

transcript: You said you were looking for a foundry.
Just telling the story of how you
first returned back to Taiwan...
I see, I see.
...and built the relation with TSMC.
You know, Windows 95.
This is too important to me.
TSMC or that?
No, I can't talk.
Okay, yeah.
Priorities in life.
Lex, I will share this with you in a second,
but this is too important to me.
There we go.

reviewNote: The humor depends on the question and response staying together. Lex is trying to resume the TSMC story while Jensen enjoys his breakfast. It is a momentary, playful pause, not a statement that the food matters more than the relationship they are discussing.
